var.explanation: Declares a function-scoped or global variable. It can be reassigned and is hoisted; modern TypeScript usually prefers let or const.

let.explanation: Declares a block-scoped variable whose value can be reassigned later.

const.explanation: Declares a block-scoped variable that cannot be reassigned after initialization. Object and array contents may still be mutated unless their types prevent it.

function.explanation: Defines a reusable block of code. In TypeScript, parameters and return values can be typed.

return.explanation: Exits a function and optionally sends a value back to the caller.

if.explanation: Runs a block of code only when a condition is true.

else.explanation: Runs a block of code when the preceding if or else-if condition was false.

else if.explanation: Checks another condition after a previous if condition was false. It is a common syntax pattern, not one single keyword.

for.explanation: Creates a loop, commonly with initialization, condition, and step expressions.

for...of.explanation: Loops over values from an iterable such as an array, string, Map, or Set.

for...in.explanation: Loops over enumerable property names of an object.

while.explanation: Repeats a block while a condition remains true; the condition is checked before each iteration.

do.explanation: Starts a do-while loop, where the body runs once before the condition is checked.

do...while.explanation: A loop pattern using do and while where the body executes at least once.

switch.explanation: Compares a value against several cases and runs the matching branch.

case.explanation: Defines one branch inside a switch statement.

default.explanation: Defines the fallback branch in a switch statement, or the default export from a module.

break.explanation: Immediately exits the nearest loop or switch statement.

continue.explanation: Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next one.

try.explanation: Marks a block of code whose errors can be handled by catch or cleaned up with finally.

catch.explanation: Handles an exception thrown inside the matching try block.

finally.explanation: Runs after try/catch whether or not an error happened.

throw.explanation: Raises an error and stops normal execution unless the error is caught.

class.explanation: Defines a blueprint for creating objects. TypeScript adds type checking for fields, methods, constructors, visibility, and inheritance.

extends.explanation: Makes a class inherit from a parent class. In TypeScript it also constrains generics and extends interfaces/types in certain contexts.

constructor.explanation: A special class method that runs when a new instance is created.

this.explanation: Refers to the current execution context or object instance. TypeScript can type-check this in methods and functions.

super.explanation: Calls or accesses members from a parent class inside a subclass.

new.explanation: Creates a new object from a class or constructor function.

static.explanation: Defines a class member that belongs to the class itself instead of instances.

import.explanation: Imports values from another module. TypeScript also supports type-only imports.
import.example:
import { add } from './math';
import type { User } from './types';

export.explanation: Exports values or types from a module so other files can import them.

from.explanation: Used in import/export declarations to specify the source module.

as.explanation: Renames imports/exports in JavaScript, and performs type assertions or type remapping in TypeScript.
as.example:
import { readFile as read } from 'node:fs/promises';
const input = document.getElementById('name') as HTMLInputElement;

async.explanation: Marks a function as asynchronous. It returns a Promise and can use await inside.

await.explanation: Waits for a Promise to settle and gives the resolved value inside async code or supported modules.

yield.explanation: Pauses a generator function and produces a value to the caller.

typeof.explanation: At runtime, returns a string describing a value's JavaScript type. In TypeScript type positions, gets the type of a value.
typeof.example:
const x = 42;
type XType = typeof x; // number

instanceof.explanation: Checks at runtime whether an object is an instance of a class or constructor.

in.explanation: Checks whether a property exists in an object, and can also help TypeScript narrow union types.

delete.explanation: Removes a property from an object.
delete.example:
const user: { name?: string } = { name: 'Nina' };
delete user.name;

void.explanation: In TypeScript, usually means a function returns no meaningful value. In JavaScript, void evaluates an expression and returns undefined.

debugger.explanation: Places a breakpoint for debugging tools when execution reaches it.

with.explanation: A legacy JavaScript statement that extends the scope chain. It is forbidden in strict mode and should not be used.
with.example: // Avoid using with in TypeScript/modern JavaScript.

interface.explanation: Describes the shape an object must have, including property and method names and their types.

type.explanation: Creates a reusable type alias for any type expression, such as unions, intersections, tuples, objects, and function types.
type.example:
type ID = string | number;
let userId: ID = 42;

enum.explanation: Defines a set of named constants. TypeScript emits runtime JavaScript for normal enums.
enum.example:
enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }
const c: Color = Color.Green;

const enum.explanation: Defines an enum that TypeScript tries to inline at compile time instead of emitting a runtime enum object.
const enum.example:
const enum Direction { Up, Down }
const d = Direction.Up;

implements.explanation: Declares that a class must provide the members required by an interface or type shape.

namespace.explanation: Groups related code under a named container. Modern TypeScript often prefers ES modules, but namespaces are still supported.

module.explanation: A TypeScript declaration construct used for ambient external modules and legacy internal module syntax. In Node/CommonJS, use module.exports as the runtime object instead.

declare.explanation: Tells TypeScript that a variable, function, class, module, or type exists elsewhere without generating JavaScript output.
declare.example:
declare const VERSION: string;
declare function track(event: string): void;

global.explanation: Used in declaration files with declare global to add names to the global scope.

public.explanation: Marks a class member as accessible from anywhere. This is the default visibility in TypeScript classes.

private.explanation: Marks a class member as accessible only inside the class that declares it.

protected.explanation: Marks a class member as accessible inside the declaring class and its subclasses, but not from outside.

readonly.explanation: Marks a property or index signature as not assignable after initialization.

abstract.explanation: Marks a class or member as incomplete and intended to be implemented by subclasses.

override.explanation: Marks a subclass method or property as intentionally overriding a member from a base class.

accessor.explanation: Declares an auto-accessor class member, generating getter/setter behavior with TypeScript support.

get.explanation: Defines a getter method that is accessed like a property.

set.explanation: Defines a setter method that runs when a property-like assignment happens.

keyof.explanation: Produces a union of the property names of a type.
keyof.example:
interface Point { x: number; y: number; }
type PointKey = keyof Point; // 'x' | 'y'

typeof type operator.explanation: In a type position, captures the static type of a value or variable.
typeof type operator.example:
const user = { id: 1, name: 'Nina' };
type User = typeof user;

indexed access type.explanation: Uses T[K] to look up the type of a property or element.
indexed access type.example:
type User = { name: string; age: number };
type Name = User['name']; // string

conditional type.explanation: Chooses one type or another using a type-level condition with extends.
conditional type.example: type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

infer.explanation: Introduces a type variable inside a conditional type to extract part of another type.
infer.example:
type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T;
type X = ElementType<string[]>; // string

mapped type.explanation: Creates a new object type by transforming each key in another type.
mapped type.example: type Readonlyish<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };

template literal type.explanation: Builds string literal types using template literal syntax at the type level.
template literal type.example:
type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`;
type Click = EventName<'click'>; // 'onClick'

satisfies.explanation: Checks that an expression matches a type while preserving the expression's more specific inferred type.
satisfies.example: const config = { mode: 'dark' } satisfies { mode: string };

asserts.explanation: Declares that a function narrows or asserts a condition when it returns successfully.

is.explanation: Used in a type predicate to tell TypeScript how a function narrows a value.

unique.explanation: Used with symbol to create a unique symbol type for strongly typed symbolic keys.
unique.example:
const token: unique symbol = Symbol('token');
type Token = typeof token;

unique symbol.explanation: A subtype of symbol where each declaration has a distinct type identity.
unique symbol.example:
declare const ID: unique symbol;
type ID = typeof ID;

import type.explanation: Imports only types and erases the import from emitted JavaScript when possible.

export type.explanation: Exports only a type alias, interface, or other type-only declaration.

as const.explanation: A const assertion that narrows literals and makes object/array properties readonly.
as const.example:
const roles = ['admin', 'user'] as const;
type Role = typeof roles[number];

as any.explanation: A type assertion that forces a value into any, disabling type checking for that value.
as any.example:
const unsafe = value as any;
unsafe.anything();

non-null assertion.explanation: The postfix ! tells TypeScript to treat a value as not null or undefined.

definite assignment assertion.explanation: The ! on a class property tells TypeScript it will be assigned before use, even if not assigned in the constructor.

optional property.explanation: The ? after a property name marks it as optional.

optional parameter.explanation: The ? after a parameter name marks it as optional.

parameter property.explanation: A constructor parameter with a visibility or readonly modifier automatically becomes a class property.

generic constraint.explanation: Uses extends to restrict which types a generic parameter can accept.

generic default.explanation: Provides a default type for a generic parameter.
generic default.example: type ApiResponse<T = unknown> = { data: T; ok: boolean };

const type parameter.explanation: A generic type parameter modifier that helps preserve literal types for inference.

using.explanation: Declares a disposable resource for explicit resource management in supported ECMAScript/TypeScript targets.
using.example:
using file = openFile();
// disposed automatically at end of scope

await using.explanation: Declares an async-disposable resource whose cleanup is awaited at the end of scope.

decorator.explanation: An @ expression applied to a class or class member to add metadata or transform behavior when decorators are enabled.

@.explanation: Decorator prefix used before a decorator expression.

declare module.explanation: Declares the types for an external module, often in .d.ts files.

declare global.explanation: Augments global types from inside a module declaration file.

ambient declaration.explanation: A declaration that describes existing runtime code without emitting JavaScript.
ambient declaration.example: declare const process: { env: Record<string, string | undefined> };

triple-slash directive.explanation: A /// directive that gives the TypeScript compiler extra file, type, or lib information.

// @ts-ignore.explanation: Suppresses the next line's TypeScript error without checking that an error actually exists.

// @ts-expect-error.explanation: Suppresses the next line's TypeScript error and reports an error if no TypeScript error exists.

// @ts-check.explanation: Enables TypeScript checking in a JavaScript file.

// @ts-nocheck.explanation: Disables TypeScript checking for an entire file.

number.explanation: Represents JavaScript numbers, including integers and floating-point values.
number.example:
let age: number = 37;
let price: number = 19.99;

bigint.explanation: Represents arbitrary-size integer values using JavaScript BigInt.

symbol.explanation: Represents JavaScript symbol values, commonly used as unique object keys.

object.explanation: Represents non-primitive values, such as arrays, functions, and plain objects.

undefined.explanation: Represents the JavaScript value undefined, often meaning no value has been assigned.

null.explanation: Represents an intentional empty value. With strictNullChecks, null must be included in a type explicitly.

true.explanation: The boolean literal value true. It can also be used as a literal type.

false.explanation: The boolean literal value false. It can also be used as a literal type.

any.explanation: Disables type checking for a value. Useful as an escape hatch, but removes TypeScript safety.

unknown.explanation: A safer top type: any value can be assigned to unknown, but it must be narrowed before use.

never.explanation: Represents values that should never occur, often for functions that always throw or exhaustive checks.

void type.explanation: A function return type meaning callers should not use a returned value.

literal type.explanation: A type that allows only a specific literal value, such as a specific string, number, boolean, or bigint.

union type.explanation: Combines multiple possible types with |, so a value can be any one of them.

intersection type.explanation: Combines multiple types with &, so a value must satisfy all of them.

tuple.explanation: An array type with a fixed number of positions and known types for each position.

readonly tuple.explanation: A tuple whose elements cannot be reassigned.

array type.explanation: Represents a list of values of the same type.
array type.example:
let scores: number[] = [90, 85, 100];
let names: Array<string> = ['Nina', 'Alex'];

function type.explanation: Describes the parameter and return types of a function value.
function type.example:
type Add = (a: number, b: number) => number;
const add: Add = (a, b) => a + b;

construct signature.explanation: Describes a type that can be called with new.

index signature.explanation: Describes property types for keys that are not known in advance.

discriminated union.explanation: A union where each member has a shared literal property used to narrow the exact case.

recursive type.explanation: A type that refers to itself, often used for trees or nested data.
recursive type.example: type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json };

=>.explanation: Arrow function: a shorter way to write a function. With one expression the result is returned automatically.

?.explanation: When used after a property or parameter name, marks it as optional in TypeScript.

!.explanation: Non-null assertion: tells the compiler "trust me, this is not null". It changes NOTHING at runtime, so if you are wrong the program still crashes.

?..explanation: Optional chaining: read a property only if the thing exists, instead of throwing.

??.explanation: Nullish coalescing: use the right side only when the left is null or undefined. Unlike || , it keeps 0 and "" .
??.example:
const count = input ?? 0;   // 0 stays 0
const bad = 0 || 5;         // 5 - probably not wanted

??=.explanation: Nullish assignment assigns the right side only when the left side is null or undefined.

||.explanation: Logical OR: true when either side is true. Careful as a default value - it replaces 0 and "" too; ?? does not.

&&.explanation: Logical AND: true only when both sides are true. Stops at the first false side.

||=.explanation: Logical OR assignment assigns only when the left side is falsy.

&&=.explanation: Logical AND assignment assigns only when the left side is truthy.

===.explanation: Strict equality: equal AND the same type. Prefer this over == , which converts types first and produces surprises like "" == 0 being true.

!==.explanation: Strict inequality: different in value OR in type.

==.explanation: Loose equality: converts the two sides to a common type BEFORE comparing, which makes "" == 0 and "1" == 1 both true. Use === unless you specifically want that.

!=.explanation: Loose inequality compares values with JavaScript type coercion. Prefer !== in most TypeScript code.

....explanation: Spread or rest: spreads a list into separate items, or collects separate items into a list.

spread.explanation: The ... syntax used to expand arrays or objects into another array/object or function call.

rest parameter.explanation: The ... syntax in a function parameter list that collects extra arguments into an array.

destructuring.explanation: Extracts values from arrays or objects into variables.
destructuring.example:
const { name, age } = user;
const [first, second] = values;

template literal.explanation: A backtick string that supports interpolation with ${...} and multi-line text.

optional chaining.explanation: Safe property access/call/index syntax using ?., returning undefined instead of throwing on nullish values.

nullish coalescing.explanation: Uses ?? to provide a fallback only for null or undefined.

ternary operator.explanation: A conditional expression that chooses between two expressions.

destructured parameter.explanation: A function parameter that destructures an object or array and can be typed inline.

Object.explanation: The base constructor and namespace for object-related methods.

Array.explanation: The JavaScript array constructor and type for ordered lists.

String.explanation: The boxed String constructor and namespace for string conversion. Prefer the primitive type string for annotations.
String.example:
const s = String(42);
let name: string = 'Nina';

Number.explanation: The boxed Number constructor and number utility namespace. Prefer the primitive type number for annotations.

Boolean.explanation: The boxed Boolean constructor. Prefer the primitive type boolean for annotations.
Boolean.example:
const b = Boolean(value);
let ok: boolean = true;

BigInt.explanation: Creates bigint values from integers or strings.

Math.explanation: Provides common mathematical constants and functions.
Math.example:
const radius = 3;
const area = Math.PI * radius ** 2;

JSON.explanation: Provides JSON parsing and serialization functions.
JSON.example:
const data = JSON.parse('{"ok":true}') as { ok: boolean };
const text = JSON.stringify(data);

RegExp.explanation: Represents regular expressions for pattern matching strings.

Promise.explanation: Represents a value that may be available later after an asynchronous operation.

Map.explanation: Stores key-value pairs where keys can be any value.
Map.example:
const scores = new Map<string, number>();
scores.set('Nina', 100);

WeakMap.explanation: Stores weakly held object keys mapped to values, allowing garbage collection.

WeakSet.explanation: Stores weakly held object values, allowing garbage collection.

Error.explanation: Base class for JavaScript runtime errors.

TypeError.explanation: Error thrown when a value is not of the expected runtime type.

ReferenceError.explanation: Error thrown when code references a variable that does not exist.

RangeError.explanation: Error thrown when a numeric value is outside an allowed range.

SyntaxError.explanation: Error thrown when code or parsed text has invalid syntax.
SyntaxError.example: try { JSON.parse('{bad'); } catch (err) { console.log(err instanceof SyntaxError); }

URIError.explanation: Error thrown by URI encoding/decoding functions when input is invalid.
URIError.example: try { decodeURIComponent('%'); } catch (err) { console.log(err instanceof URIError); }

EvalError.explanation: Legacy error type related to eval. Rarely used in modern code.

AggregateError.explanation: Represents multiple errors grouped into one error object.
AggregateError.example: throw new AggregateError([new Error('A'), new Error('B')], 'Many errors');

ArrayBuffer.explanation: Represents a fixed-length raw binary data buffer.

DataView.explanation: Reads and writes multiple number types from an ArrayBuffer.
DataView.example:
const view = new DataView(new ArrayBuffer(8));
view.setInt32(0, 123);

Int8Array.explanation: A typed array for signed 8-bit integers.

Uint8Array.explanation: A typed array for unsigned 8-bit integers.

Uint8ClampedArray.explanation: A typed array for unsigned 8-bit integers clamped between 0 and 255.

Int16Array.explanation: A typed array for signed 16-bit integers.

Uint16Array.explanation: A typed array for unsigned 16-bit integers.

Int32Array.explanation: A typed array for signed 32-bit integers.

Uint32Array.explanation: A typed array for unsigned 32-bit integers.

Float32Array.explanation: A typed array for 32-bit floating-point numbers.

Float64Array.explanation: A typed array for 64-bit floating-point numbers.

BigInt64Array.explanation: A typed array for signed 64-bit bigint values.

BigUint64Array.explanation: A typed array for unsigned 64-bit bigint values.

console.explanation: Common runtime object for logging messages in browsers and Node.js.

fetch.explanation: Common Web/API function for making HTTP requests. Available in browsers and modern Node runtimes with appropriate libs.
fetch.example:
const res = await fetch('/api/users');
const users = await res.json();

setTimeout.explanation: Runs a callback after a delay.

setInterval.explanation: Runs a callback repeatedly after a delay interval.

clearTimeout.explanation: Cancels a timeout created by setTimeout.

clearInterval.explanation: Cancels an interval created by setInterval.

queueMicrotask.explanation: Queues a function to run as a microtask after the current task completes.

parseInt.explanation: Parses a string and returns an integer.

parseFloat.explanation: Parses a string and returns a floating-point number.

isNaN.explanation: Checks whether a value is NaN after coercion. Prefer Number.isNaN for stricter checks.

isFinite.explanation: Checks whether a value is finite after coercion. Prefer Number.isFinite for stricter checks.

encodeURI.explanation: Encodes a full URI by escaping characters where needed.

decodeURI.explanation: Decodes a URI previously encoded with encodeURI.

encodeURIComponent.explanation: Encodes a URI component such as a query parameter value.

globalThis.explanation: Standard global object reference that works across environments.

window.explanation: The browser global object for a window/tab. Available when DOM libs are included.

document.explanation: The browser DOM document object. Available when DOM libs are included.

HTMLElement.explanation: Base DOM type for HTML elements.

HTMLInputElement.explanation: DOM type for input elements, exposing properties like value and checked.
HTMLInputElement.example:
const input = document.querySelector('input') as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(input.value);

MouseEvent.explanation: DOM event type for mouse interactions.

KeyboardEvent.explanation: DOM event type for keyboard interactions.

Response.explanation: Type for HTTP responses returned by fetch.

Headers.explanation: Type for HTTP headers used with fetch requests and responses.

Partial.explanation: Makes all properties of a type optional.

Required.explanation: Makes all properties of a type required.

Readonly.explanation: Makes all properties of a type readonly.

Record.explanation: Creates an object type with keys K and values T.

Pick.explanation: Creates a type by selecting specific properties from another type.

Omit.explanation: Creates a type by removing specific properties from another type.

Exclude.explanation: Removes union members that are assignable to another type.
Exclude.example: type NonNullish = Exclude<string | null | undefined, null | undefined>;

Extract.explanation: Keeps union members that are assignable to another type.
Extract.example: type Strings = Extract<string | number | boolean, string>;

NonNullable.explanation: Removes null and undefined from a type.

Parameters.explanation: Gets a tuple of a function type's parameter types.
Parameters.example: type Args = Parameters<(a: string, b: number) => void>;

ConstructorParameters.explanation: Gets a tuple of constructor parameter types from a class/constructor type.

ReturnType.explanation: Gets the return type of a function type.

InstanceType.explanation: Gets the instance type created by a constructor type.

NoInfer.explanation: Blocks inference into a type position so another source controls the generic type.

ThisParameterType.explanation: Extracts the type of a function's this parameter.
ThisParameterType.example:
function f(this: Date) { return this.getTime(); }
type T = ThisParameterType<typeof f>;

OmitThisParameter.explanation: Removes the this parameter from a function type.

ThisType.explanation: Marks the contextual this type for object literals. It is a marker interface.

Awaited.explanation: Recursively unwraps the resolved type of a Promise-like value.

Uppercase.explanation: Converts a string literal type to uppercase.

Lowercase.explanation: Converts a string literal type to lowercase.

Capitalize.explanation: Capitalizes the first character of a string literal type.

Uncapitalize.explanation: Lowercases the first character of a string literal type.

ArrayLike.explanation: Describes an object with numeric indexes and a length, similar to an array but not necessarily an Array.

ReadonlyArray.explanation: An array type whose elements cannot be modified through that reference.

PromiseLike.explanation: Describes values that behave like Promises because they have a then method.

Iterable.explanation: Describes values that can be iterated with for...of.

Iterator.explanation: Describes an object that produces values one at a time through next().

Generator.explanation: A type for generator objects returned from generator functions.

AsyncIterable.explanation: Describes values that can be iterated asynchronously with for await...of.

AsyncIterator.explanation: Describes an async iterator object whose next method returns promises.

AsyncGenerator.explanation: A type for async generator objects returned from async generator functions.

PropertyKey.explanation: A built-in alias for string | number | symbol, the valid JavaScript property key types.

Function.explanation: The broad type for callable JavaScript Function objects. Prefer specific function types when possible.

CallableFunction.explanation: Library interface for callable function objects with stronger call/apply/bind typing.

NewableFunction.explanation: Library interface for constructor-like function objects.

IArguments.explanation: Type for the legacy arguments object inside non-arrow functions.

ReadonlyMap.explanation: A Map type exposed through read-only methods.
ReadonlyMap.example: const m: ReadonlyMap<string, number> = new Map([['a', 1]]);

ReadonlySet.explanation: A Set type exposed through read-only methods.

WeakRef.explanation: Represents a weak reference to an object, if the target environment includes it.
WeakRef.example:
const ref = new WeakRef({ value: 1 });
const value = ref.deref();

FinalizationRegistry.explanation: Registers cleanup callbacks that may run after objects are garbage-collected.

Disposable.explanation: Interface for explicitly disposable resources used by using declarations.

AsyncDisposable.explanation: Interface for resources that need asynchronous cleanup with await using.

require.explanation: CommonJS function for importing modules in Node.js. ES module import is preferred in modern TypeScript when possible.

exports.explanation: CommonJS shortcut for adding named exports to module.exports.
exports.example: exports.add = (a: number, b: number) => a + b;

process.explanation: Node.js global object containing process information, environment variables, and exit controls.

Buffer.explanation: Node.js class for working with binary data.

__dirname.explanation: CommonJS variable containing the current module directory path.

__filename.explanation: CommonJS variable containing the current module file path.

NodeJS.explanation: Namespace commonly provided by @types/node for Node-specific TypeScript types.

global namespace.explanation: The top-level namespace where globally available types and values live.

ES module.explanation: A file using import/export syntax with its own module scope.
ES module.example:
export const version = '1.0.0';
import { version } from './version';

CommonJS.explanation: Node's older module system based on require and module.exports.

.d.ts.explanation: A TypeScript declaration file that describes types for JavaScript or generated code without implementation.
.d.ts.example:
// index.d.ts
export interface User { id: string; }

tsconfig.json.explanation: TypeScript project configuration file that controls compiler options and included files.

strict.explanation: Compiler option family that enables stronger type checking rules.

noImplicitAny.explanation: Reports an error when TypeScript would infer any implicitly.

strictNullChecks.explanation: Makes null and undefined distinct types that must be handled explicitly.

target.explanation: Sets the JavaScript language version TypeScript emits.

module compiler option.explanation: Controls the emitted module format or module behavior.

lib.explanation: Chooses which built-in library declarations are included, such as DOM or ES2023.

jsx.explanation: Controls JSX parsing/emission for React or other JSX runtimes.

types.explanation: Limits which @types packages are included globally.

paths.explanation: Defines import path aliases when used with baseUrl/module resolution.

Array.map.explanation: Creates a new array by transforming each item.

Array.filter.explanation: Creates a new array containing only items that pass a test.

Array.reduce.explanation: Combines array items into one accumulated value.
Array.reduce.example: const total = nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);

Array.find.explanation: Returns the first array item that matches a predicate, or undefined.

Array.includes.explanation: Checks whether an array contains a value.

String.includes.explanation: Checks whether a string contains a substring.

String.split.explanation: Splits a string into an array of substrings.

String.trim.explanation: Removes whitespace from both ends of a string.

Promise.all.explanation: Waits for all promises to resolve or rejects when one rejects.

Promise.race.explanation: Settles as soon as the first promise settles.

Promise.allSettled.explanation: Waits for all promises to settle and returns status objects for each one.

Promise.any.explanation: Resolves with the first fulfilled promise, or rejects if all reject.

package.explanation: Reserved in strict JavaScript/TypeScript contexts; not used as a normal variable name.

eval.explanation: A built-in function name that is restricted in strict mode and should not be used as a variable name.
eval.example:
// Avoid shadowing eval.
const result = eval('1 + 1');

arguments.explanation: A special function-local object in non-arrow functions; restricted as a binding name in strict mode.

module.exports.explanation: CommonJS export object used in Node.js to define what a module exports at runtime.

import = require.explanation: TypeScript syntax for importing CommonJS or export= modules in declaration-compatible code.

export =.explanation: TypeScript syntax used in declaration files for modules that export a single CommonJS-style value.
export =.example:
declare function createApp(): App;
export = createApp;

import defer.explanation: Deferred module import syntax supported by TypeScript for ECMAScript's deferred module evaluation proposal.

defer.explanation: Used as part of import defer syntax to delay module evaluation until the namespace is accessed.

out.explanation: Variance annotation for generic type parameters, marking a type parameter as covariant in supported positions.

in variance.explanation: Variance annotation pattern for generic type parameters, marking a type parameter as contravariant in supported positions.

in out.explanation: Variance annotation pattern for generic type parameters that are both input and output positions.

intrinsic.explanation: A special marker used internally by TypeScript for compiler-provided intrinsic string manipulation types.

Symbol.dispose.explanation: Well-known symbol used by explicit resource management for synchronous disposal.

Symbol.asyncDispose.explanation: Well-known symbol used by explicit resource management for asynchronous disposal.

import attributes.explanation: Module import metadata syntax, commonly used for things like JSON module loading depending on runtime/tooling support.

with import attribute.explanation: The with clause used in import attributes, not to be confused with the legacy JavaScript with statement.

type assertion.explanation: Syntax that tells TypeScript to treat a value as a specific type. Prefer as syntax in TSX-compatible code.

angle-bracket assertion.explanation: Older type assertion syntax using <Type>value. It cannot be used in TSX files because it conflicts with JSX.

%.explanation: Remainder (modulo): what is left over after division. n % 2 === 0 means n is even.

**.explanation: Power: raises the left number to the power of the right one.

++.explanation: Adds one to a variable, in place.

+=.explanation: Adds to a variable and stores the result back in it.

=.explanation: Assignment: puts the value on the right into the name on the left. To COMPARE use === .

?:.explanation: Marks a property or parameter as optional: it may be missing entirely.
?:.example: interface User { name: string; nickname?: string }
